dedupe_keys.name: hurricane harvey impact on medicare home health care use in texas interrupted time series 2017 to 2018

description: This case study measures how Hurricane Harvey, which struck Texas in August 2017, disrupted home health care for older people. Chih-Ying Li and colleagues at the University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston and the University of Washington published it in the Journal of Applied Gerontology in 2026. They linked patient-level Medicare home health claims for 2017 and 2018 with county disaster declarations from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and used segmented interrupted time series to estimate monthly changes in home health use among 142,416 beneficiaries in affected and unaffected counties, both immediately after landfall and in the following months. The article is available online, free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial licence. Coverage is Texas. Caveats: Medicare claims are restricted data not shared with the article, and similar drops in unaffected counties complicate attribution. Home health nursing use fell 16 percent immediately after the hurricane and kept falling slightly through the post-Harvey period in affected counties, but similar changes appeared in unaffected counties; therapy use fell less, and beneficiaries with the lowest function saw larger immediate drops in therapy in affected counties. The authors call for stronger mandatory disaster preparedness rules for Medicare-certified home health agencies. Simulation uses: service disruption magnitudes for home-based care in hurricane impact and recovery models. Related records: the post-hurricane supply chains study for Harvey, Irma and Maria (case_study-post-hurricane-supply-chains-harvey-irma-maria) covers other Harvey service disruptions.
